It is appropriate for preventing a side-effecting tool from executing. respond treats the human’s message as a successful synthetic tool result and is intended for ask-user style interactions. It should not be used to deny a consequential operation.

Q5. How should HITL be secured in production?

The application should authenticate reviewers, authorize them for the affected resource, display the complete proposed action, validate edited arguments, apply approval expiration, prevent duplicate resumes, and use idempotency for side effects. It should also preserve an audit trail containing the original proposal, reviewer identity, decision, modifications, timestamp, execution outcome, and relevant correlation identifiers.


Topic 9: Agent Error Recovery

Agent Error Recovery enables an agent to detect failures, classify their causes, choose an appropriate recovery strategy, and either continue safely or terminate with a controlled response. Recovery may involve retrying transient failures, correcting tool arguments, selecting an alternative tool or model, requesting human input, replanning the workflow, or stopping execution.

Modern framework note: Current LangChain supports recovery through middleware such as ToolRetryMiddleware, ToolErrorMiddleware, ModelFallbackMiddleware, ModelCallLimitMiddleware, and ToolCallLimitMiddleware. These components run inside the compiled LangGraph returned by create_agent().

a) Definition

Agent Error Recovery is the process through which an agent responds to failures occurring during model calls, tool selection, argument generation, tool execution, state updates, planning, or final-response generation. Instead of allowing every exception to terminate the workflow immediately, the agent determines whether an alternative action can complete the task safely.

Recovery begins by classifying an error according to its cause and recoverability. A temporary network timeout may justify an automatic retry, malformed tool arguments may be corrected by the model, missing user information may require clarification, and a permission denial should normally terminate the requested action immediately.

Recovery can occur at several levels of the agent architecture. The system may retry the same tool, select another tool, fall back to another model, revise the plan, restore an earlier checkpoint, ask a human for guidance, or return a controlled error response.

A production recovery process must be bounded and observable. Every retry, fallback, replan, and human escalation should have limits, because an uncontrolled recovery loop can increase latency, cost, resource usage, and the possibility of repeated external side effects.

b) Purpose

The primary purpose of Agent Error Recovery is to help an agent continue operating when it encounters a temporary or correctable failure. External APIs may time out, models may produce malformed arguments, databases may temporarily reject connections, and retrieval tools may return incomplete results, but these failures do not always require the complete workflow to stop.

Recovery allows different categories of failures to receive different responses instead of applying one generic strategy to every exception. Transient infrastructure failures can be retried automatically, model-correctable failures can be returned as tool observations, unclear requests can be escalated to the user, and unexpected programming errors can propagate to developers for investigation.

The recovery process protects external systems from unsafe or repeated operations. A write operation should not be retried automatically unless it is idempotent, and authorization failures, validation errors, missing resources, or business-rule violations should not be treated as temporary service failures.

Error recovery improves reliability and observability by recording how the workflow responded to each failure. Applications can track the failing component, error category, retry count, fallback selection, human escalation, execution duration, and final outcome without exposing internal credentials, private data, or raw stack traces to the user.

c) Architecture Diagram

                   AGENT ERROR RECOVERY
                   ====================

                       User Request
                            |
                            v
                         Agent
                            |
                            v
                    Model or Tool Call
                            |
                            v
                      Did it succeed?
                     /              \
                   Yes               No
                    |                 |
                    v                 v
             Continue workflow   Classify error
                                      |
                 +--------------------+--------------------+
                 |                    |                    |
                 v                    v                    v
             Transient          Model-correctable    User-fixable
                 |                    |                    |
                 v                    v                    v
          Bounded retry       Error ToolMessage      Ask user or
          with backoff        and self-correction    human review
                 |
                 v
          Retry exhausted?
             /       \
           No         Yes
           |           |
           v           v
        Retry       Fallback tool,
                    fallback model,
                    or safe failure
                          |
                          v
                   Update agent state
                          |
                          v
                   Continue or terminate

Architecture Explanation

The agent first attempts its normal model or tool operation. If the operation succeeds, the result is added to the agent state and the workflow proceeds normally.

When a failure occurs, the recovery layer classifies it before choosing an action. This classification prevents permanent failures such as invalid permissions from entering a retry loop intended for temporary network problems.

Transient failures are retried using bounded attempts and backoff. Current LangChain fault-tolerance guidance recommends automatic retries for temporary network failures and rate limits, while model-correctable tool problems can be returned as error ToolMessage observations.

User-fixable failures should pause the workflow and request missing information or human intervention. A model should not invent an account ID, approval, resource name, or other required value merely to keep the workflow running.

Unexpected internal errors should normally propagate to the application rather than being converted into misleading recoverable observations. LangChain’s fault-tolerance guidance explicitly distinguishes unexpected developer errors from failures intended for automatic recovery.

d) Core Components

1. Error Classifier

The error classifier identifies the type and recoverability of a failure before the agent chooses a response. It distinguishes transient infrastructure problems, model-correctable tool errors, user-fixable requests, authorization failures, and unexpected internal defects. Classification should rely on exception types, status codes, error codes, and structured results rather than fragile string matching whenever possible. Accurate classification prevents unnecessary retries and ensures that permanent or unsafe failures terminate correctly.

2. Retry Policy

The retry policy determines which failures may be attempted again, how many attempts are allowed, and how long the system waits between attempts. Temporary timeouts, connection failures, and selected rate-limit errors are common retry candidates. The policy must exclude permanent failures and unsafe side effects. Validation errors, permission denials, missing resources, and non-idempotent write operations should not normally be retried unchanged.

3. Error Observation

An error observation communicates a recoverable failure back to the agent through structured state or an error ToolMessage. It should clearly state what failed and what correction is possible without exposing secrets or raw internal stack traces. The model can use the observation to revise arguments, choose another tool, or explain the failure. The application must limit correction attempts so the model cannot repeat the same failing operation indefinitely.

4. Fallback Strategy

A fallback strategy provides an approved alternative when the primary model, tool, or retrieval source remains unavailable. The alternative should offer compatible functionality and return data in a format the remaining workflow can interpret. Fallbacks should be explicit and observable rather than silently changing system behavior. The execution trace should record which primary component failed, which fallback was chosen, and whether the fallback result satisfied the original requirement.

5. Recovery Limits

Recovery limits restrict the number of retries, model corrections, tool calls, replans, and fallback attempts allowed during one agent run. These limits prevent runaway loops, excessive cost, and repeated pressure on an unavailable dependency. When a limit is reached, the workflow should terminate with a controlled status or escalate for human review. It should not silently return incomplete work as a successfully recovered result.

d) Code Example

from typing import Literal, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph


class AgentState(TypedDict):
    order_id: str
    status: str
    result: dict | None
    error: str | None
    attempts: int
    max_attempts: int
    recovery_action: Literal[
        "none",
        "retry",
        "fallback",
        "stop",
    ]
    final_answer: str


class TemporaryServiceError(Exception):
    """Raised when the primary service is unavailable."""


primary_attempts: dict[str, int] = {}


def primary_order_service(
    order_id: str,
) -> dict:
    """
    Simulate a primary service that always fails.

    This demonstrates retry exhaustion and fallback.
    """

    current_attempt = primary_attempts.get(
        order_id,
        0,
    )

    primary_attempts[order_id] = (
        current_attempt + 1
    )

    raise TemporaryServiceError(
        "The primary order service is unavailable."
    )


def fallback_order_service(
    order_id: str,
) -> dict:
    """Simulate an approved fallback data source."""

    fallback_database = {
        "ORD-1001": {
            "status": "Shipped",
            "source": "fallback-cache",
        }
    }

    order = fallback_database.get(
        order_id
    )

    if order is None:
        return {
            "found": False,
            "order_id": order_id,
            "source": "fallback-cache",
        }

    return {
        "found": True,
        "order_id": order_id,
        "status": order["status"],
        "source": order["source"],
    }


def call_primary_service(
    state: AgentState,
) -> dict:
    """Attempt the primary operation."""

    attempt = state["attempts"] + 1

    try:
        result = primary_order_service(
            state["order_id"]
        )

        return {
            "status": "primary_success",
            "result": result,
            "error": None,
            "attempts": attempt,
            "recovery_action": "none",
        }

    except TemporaryServiceError:
        return {
            "status": "primary_failed",
            "result": None,
            "error": (
                "The primary order service is "
                "temporarily unavailable."
            ),
            "attempts": attempt,
            "recovery_action": "none",
        }


def decide_recovery(
    state: AgentState,
) -> str:
    """
    Retry while attempts remain.

    Use fallback after the retry budget is exhausted.
    """

    if state["status"] == "primary_success":
        return "finish"

    if state["attempts"] < state["max_attempts"\]:
        return "retry"

    return "fallback"


def mark_retry(
    state: AgentState,
) -> dict:
    """Record the selected recovery action."""

    print(
        f"Primary attempt {state['attempts']} failed. "
        "Retrying."
    )

    return {
        "recovery_action": "retry",
    }


def call_fallback_service(
    state: AgentState,
) -> dict:
    """Call the approved fallback service."""

    print(
        "Retry budget exhausted. "
        "Using the fallback service."
    )

    result = fallback_order_service(
        state["order_id"]
    )

    return {
        "status": "fallback_completed",
        "result": result,
        "recovery_action": "fallback",
    }


def prepare_final_answer(
    state: AgentState,
) -> dict:
    """Create the final user-facing response."""

    result = state["result"]

    if result is None:
        answer = (
            "The order could not be retrieved."
        )

    elif result.get("found") is False:
        answer = (
            f"Order {state['order_id']} was not found."
        )

    else:
        answer = (
            f"Order {state['order_id']} is "
            f"{result['status']}. "
            f"Data source: {result['source']}."
        )

    return {
        "final_answer": answer,
    }


def build_graph():
    """Build the recovery workflow."""

    builder = StateGraph(
        AgentState
    )

    builder.add_node(
        "primary",
        call_primary_service,
    )

    builder.add_node(
        "mark_retry",
        mark_retry,
    )

    builder.add_node(
        "fallback",
        call_fallback_service,
    )

    builder.add_node(
        "finish",
        prepare_final_answer,
    )

    builder.add_edge(
        START,
        "primary",
    )

    builder.add_conditional_edges(
        "primary",
        decide_recovery,
        {
            "retry": "mark_retry",
            "fallback": "fallback",
            "finish": "finish",
        },
    )

    builder.add_edge(
        "mark_retry",
        "primary",
    )

    builder.add_edge(
        "fallback",
        "finish",
    )

    builder.add_edge(
        "finish",
        END,
    )

    return builder.compile()


def main() -> None:
    primary_attempts.clear()

    graph = build_graph()

    result = graph.invoke(
        {
            "order_id": "ORD-1001",
            "status": "not_started",
            "result": None,
            "error": None,
            "attempts": 0,
            "max_attempts": 3,
            "recovery_action": "none",
            "final_answer": "",
        }
    )

    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("AGENT RECOVERY RESULT")
    print("=" * 60)

    print(
        "Primary attempts:",
        result["attempts"],
    )

    print(
        "Recovery action:",
        result["recovery_action"],
    )

    print(
        "Last primary error:",
        result["error"],
    )

    print(
        "Retrieved result:",
        result["result"],
    )

    print(
        "Final answer:",
        result["final_answer"],
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
	main()

Code Explanation

AgentState stores the operation result, error, attempt count, retry limit, recovery decision, and final answer. Keeping recovery information in state makes the workflow observable and allows routing decisions to use structured values.

primary_order_service() simulates a consistently unavailable primary dependency. The function raises a typed TemporaryServiceError, allowing the workflow to classify the problem as retryable.

call_primary_service() converts the exception into structured state rather than allowing it to crash the complete workflow. It also increments the attempt count for every primary-service call.

decide_recovery() uses deterministic routing. It retries while attempts remain, selects the fallback after exhaustion, and proceeds directly to completion if the primary operation succeeds.

call_fallback_service() represents an approved alternative source. Its result explicitly records fallback-cache as the source instead of silently presenting fallback data as a primary-service result.

The graph terminates after the fallback result is converted into a final response. Every path leads either to another bounded retry or to the finish node, preventing an uncontrolled loop.

e) Interview Questions and Answers

Q1. What is Agent Error Recovery?

Agent Error Recovery is the process of detecting and classifying failures during agent execution and selecting an appropriate response. Recovery may include retrying a temporary failure, correcting tool arguments, using a fallback model or tool, revising the plan, requesting user input, escalating to a human, or terminating safely.

Q2. Which errors should be retried?

Temporary errors such as network timeouts, transient database failures, rate limits, and selected server errors may be retried. Validation failures, permission denials, missing resources, business-rule violations, and unsafe requests should normally not be retried unchanged.

Q3. What is the difference between ToolRetryMiddleware and ToolErrorMiddleware?

ToolRetryMiddleware automatically retries selected tool-execution failures using a bounded retry policy and optional backoff. ToolErrorMiddleware converts explicitly selected execution exceptions into error ToolMessage observations. It does not retry the failed operation by itself.

Q4. How can an agent recover from a provider outage?

The agent can use a compatible fallback model through a configured fallback policy. The fallback model should support the required context size, tool schemas, structured outputs, and safety controls. The workflow should record that a fallback was used rather than silently treating both providers as identical.

Q5. How do you prevent recovery loops?

Use: Maximum retry count, Maximum model-call count, Maximum tool-call count, Replanning limits, Duplicate-action detection, Total execution timeout
Token and cost budgets, Human escalation, Explicit safe-termination states. llCurrent LangChain includes middleware for limiting both model and tool calls during an agent run.

Chapter 8: Callbacks & Observability

Topic 1: Callback Handlers

Callback Handlers provide event-driven visibility into the execution of LangChain components. They receive lifecycle events when models, chains, tools, retrievers, agents, retries, or streamed tokens start, complete, or fail, allowing observability logic to remain separate from core application logic. 

Current framework note: LangChain provides synchronous and asynchronous callback base classes, callback managers, and a usage-metadata callback handler in langchain_core.callbacks. BaseCallbackHandler exposes hooks for models, chains, tools, retrievers, agents, retries, streamed tokens, and custom events.

a) Definition

A Callback Handler is an object that receives notifications when important execution events occur in a LangChain application. For example, a handler can be notified when a chain begins, a tool completes, a retriever fails, a model produces a token, or an agent finishes its work.

Callback Handlers follow an event-driven observer pattern. LangChain components publish lifecycle events during execution, while registered handlers subscribe to those events and perform actions such as logging, timing, token collection, metric recording, or external trace reporting.

A handler commonly extends BaseCallbackHandler for synchronous execution or AsyncCallbackHandler for asynchronous execution. Developers override only the event methods they need because the base classes already provide the expected callback interface.

Callbacks add observability without requiring logging code inside every prompt, model, tool, retriever, and chain. The application’s business logic remains focused on its actual task, while independent handlers collect operational information across multiple components.

b) Purpose

The primary purpose of Callback Handlers is to make the internal execution of an LLM application observable without tightly coupling diagnostic logic to application logic. A single handler can listen to multiple lifecycle events and record what started, what completed, how long it took, and where an error occurred.

Callback Handlers help developers debug multi-component workflows whose final output does not reveal the complete execution path. When an agent produces an incorrect answer, callbacks can show whether the problem originated in a model response, retriever result, tool execution, output parser, or earlier chain operation.

They support production measurements such as execution latency, model-call count, tool-call count, retrieval duration, failure frequency, retry count, and token streaming. These measurements can be converted into logs, metrics, alerts, dashboards, or distributed traces for continuous monitoring.

Callbacks also enable runtime behavior such as displaying streamed model tokens, forwarding events to an observability platform, collecting usage metadata, and associating nested operations with a shared request or trace identifier. This helps applications provide responsive user experiences while maintaining enough diagnostic information for troubleshooting.

       Observability Platform

Architecture Explanation

A LangChain component emits lifecycle events while processing a request. The exact events depend on the component type, such as chain, model, tool, retriever, or agent.

The callback manager distributes each event to the registered handlers. Multiple handlers can process the same event independently, allowing one handler to print diagnostics while another records metrics or exports traces.

Each handler performs its configured observational action. A handler should avoid changing the primary result unless its specific workflow explicitly requires execution control through another mechanism.

Nested operations can include run and parent-run identifiers. These identifiers allow observability systems to reconstruct relationships such as an agent run containing a model call, tool execution, and another model call.

d) Core Components

1. BaseCallbackHandler

BaseCallbackHandler is the synchronous base class used to create application-specific callback handlers. It combines lifecycle interfaces for models, chains, tools, retrievers, agents, retries, streaming tokens, and custom events, allowing developers to override only the methods relevant to their use case.

The class also exposes behavioral properties such as raise_error, run_inline, and event-specific ignore settings. These settings control whether callback failures propagate, whether the handler runs inline, and whether selected categories such as model, chain, agent, or retriever events should be ignored.

2. Event Methods

Event methods are hook functions called at defined stages of component execution. Start hooks receive information about the requested operation, end hooks receive its result, and error hooks receive the exception raised during unsuccessful execution.

A handler should implement only the event methods required for its observational purpose. A latency handler may need start, end, and error events, while a streaming user interface may primarily implement on_llm_new_token().

3. Callback Manager

The callback manager coordinates event delivery between executing LangChain components and registered handlers. It allows several handlers to receive the same lifecycle event without requiring the component to call each observational system directly.

The manager also helps preserve execution relationships through run identifiers and parent-run identifiers. These relationships allow nested operations to be reconstructed as a trace rather than appearing as unrelated log entries.

4. Runnable Configuration

Callbacks can be supplied at invocation time through the Runnable config dictionary. Runtime callbacks apply to that execution and normally propagate to nested Runnable operations, making them useful for request-specific logging or tracing.

The same configuration can carry tags and metadata that help classify the run. Values such as environment, feature, request ID, or workflow name can be forwarded with callback events, but confidential data should not be placed in model-visible or externally exported metadata.

result = chain.invoke(
    input_data,
    config={
        "callbacks": [
            handler,
        ],
        "tags": [
            "orders",
            "production",
        ],
        "metadata": {
            "request_id": "REQ-101",
        },
    },
)

e) Code Example

import time
from typing import Any
from uuid import UUID

from langchain_core.callbacks import BaseCallbackHandler
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda


class ExecutionCallbackHandler(BaseCallbackHandler):
    """Observe chain start, completion, and error events."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.start_times: dict[UUID, float] = {}

    def on_chain_start(
        self,
        serialized: dict[str, Any] | None,
        inputs: Any,
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        parent_run_id: UUID | None = None,
        tags: list[str] | None = None,
        metadata: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        self.start_times[run_id] = time.perf_counter()
        print("\nCHAIN STARTED")
        print("Run ID:", run_id)
        print("Parent run ID:", parent_run_id)
        print("Input:", inputs)
        print("Tags:", tags or [])
        print("Metadata:", metadata or {})

    def on_chain_end(
        self,
        outputs: Any,
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        parent_run_id: UUID | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        duration = self._duration_ms(run_id)
        print("\nCHAIN COMPLETED")
        print("Run ID:", run_id)
        print("Output:", outputs)
        print("Duration:", f"{duration:.2f} ms")

    def on_chain_error(
        self,
        error: BaseException,
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        parent_run_id: UUID | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        duration = self._duration_ms(run_id)
        print("\nCHAIN FAILED")
        print("Run ID:", run_id)
        print("Error type:", type(error).__name__)
        print("Duration:", f"{duration:.2f} ms")

    def _duration_ms(self, run_id: UUID) -> float:
        start = self.start_times.pop(run_id, time.perf_counter())
        return (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000


def calculate_order_total(
    data: dict[str, float],
) -> dict[str, float\]:
    """Calculate an order total after validating the input."""

    quantity = float(data["quantity"])
    unit_price = float(data["unit_price"])

    if quantity <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Quantity must be greater than zero.")

    if unit_price <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Unit price must be greater than zero.")

    return {
        "quantity": quantity,
        "unit_price": unit_price,
        "total": round(quantity * unit_price, 2),
    }


order_total_chain = RunnableLambda(
    calculate_order_total
).with_config(
    {"run_name": "calculate-order-total"}
)


def run_success_example(
    handler: ExecutionCallbackHandler,
) -> None:
    print("=" * 60)
    print("SUCCESSFUL EXECUTION")
    print("=" * 60)

    result = order_total_chain.invoke(
        {"quantity": 8, "unit_price": 1250.0},
        config={
            "callbacks": [handler],
            "tags": ["orders", "calculation"],
            "metadata": {
                "request_id": "REQ-101",
                "environment": "development",
            },
        },
    )

    print("\nApplication result:", result)


def run_failure_example(
    handler: ExecutionCallbackHandler,
) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("FAILED EXECUTION")
    print("=" * 60)

    try:
        order_total_chain.invoke(
            {"quantity": 0, "unit_price": 1250.0},
            config={
                "callbacks": [handler],
                "tags": ["orders", "validation-test"],
                "metadata": {
                    "request_id": "REQ-102",
                    "environment": "development",
                },
            },
        )
    except ValueError as error:
        print("Application safely handled the failure:", error)


def main() -> None:
    handler = ExecutionCallbackHandler()
    run_success_example(handler)
    run_failure_example(handler)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

f) Interview Questions and Answers

Q1. What is a Callback Handler in LangChain?

A Callback Handler is an object that receives notifications when important lifecycle events occur during LangChain execution. It can observe model, chain, tool, retriever, agent, token-streaming, retry, and custom events without requiring observational code inside every application component.

Q2. What is BaseCallbackHandler?

BaseCallbackHandler is the synchronous base class for implementing custom callback handlers. Developers subclass it and override only the event methods required by their application. It includes lifecycle interfaces for LLMs, chat models, chains, tools, retrievers, agents, retries, token streaming, and custom events.

Q3. What is the difference between start, end, and error callbacks?

A start callback runs immediately before a component performs its operation and can capture its inputs, metadata, and start time. An end callback runs after successful completion and receives the result, while an error callback runs when the component raises an exception.

Q4. What is the difference between runtime and constructor callbacks?

Runtime callbacks are supplied through the Runnable configuration for a particular invocation and can propagate to nested Runnable operations. Constructor callbacks are attached to a specific component instance. Runtime callbacks are often more appropriate for request-specific metadata, tracing, correlation, and conditional diagnostics.

Q5. What should be considered when using callbacks in production?

Production handlers should minimize execution overhead, use structured records, preserve run relationships, redact sensitive data, apply storage retention policies, and isolate observability-export failures from the primary workflow. Token-level events should be sampled or aggregated when appropriate because they can generate high event volumes.

Topic 2: Custom Callbacks

Custom Callbacks allow developers to create application-specific observability behavior by extending a LangChain callback base class and overriding selected lifecycle methods. They can collect structured events, measure execution duration, stream tokens, count operations, redact sensitive values, and send telemetry to external monitoring systems without modifying the core chain, tool, model, or retriever logic.

Current framework note: LangChain provides BaseCallbackHandler for synchronous handlers and AsyncCallbackHandler for asynchronous handlers. The callback interface includes lifecycle hooks for chains, chat models, LLMs, tools, retrievers, agents, retries, streams, and custom events.


a) Definition

A Custom Callback is a developer-defined handler that responds to selected LangChain lifecycle events. The handler can execute application-specific observability logic whenever a model starts, a chain completes, a tool fails, a retriever returns documents, a retry occurs, or a token is streamed. 

Custom handlers are normally created by subclassing BaseCallbackHandler or AsyncCallbackHandler. The base classes provide default implementations, so the developer needs to override only the methods required by the application.

The callback logic remains separate from the application’s primary business logic. A calculation function can focus on calculating a result, while a custom callback independently records execution time, success status, error type, tags, metadata, and run relationships.

Custom callbacks can send events to different observability destinations. The same lifecycle event can be transformed into a console message, structured log, metric, audit record, user-interface update, or trace exported to an external observability platform.

b) Purpose

The primary purpose of Custom Callbacks is to collect exactly the execution information required by a particular application instead of relying only on generic console output. An enterprise application may need request identifiers, tenant information, tool latency, failure types, retry counts, or custom business metrics that a standard handler does not capture in the required format.

Custom Callbacks allow observability behavior to be added without placing logging and monitoring code throughout every model, chain, tool, retriever, and agent function. This separation keeps the operational instrumentation reusable and prevents the main application logic from becoming tightly coupled to a specific logger, monitoring vendor, storage service, or tracing platform.

They help convert low-level lifecycle events into meaningful structured records that can support debugging, monitoring, auditing, and performance analysis. For example, a custom handler can combine a chain-start timestamp with the corresponding chain-end event to calculate latency and publish one complete execution record.

Custom Callbacks also make it possible to apply application-specific privacy and governance rules before observability information leaves the trusted runtime. Sensitive fields can be removed, masked, hashed, summarized, or excluded before prompts, tool arguments, database results, or user identifiers are sent to logs and external telemetry systems.

c) Architecture Diagram

                   ====================

                       User Request

                    LangChain Runnable
                            |
          +-----------------+-----------------+
          |                 |                 |
          v                 v                 v
       Chain Event       Tool Event       Model Event
          |                 |                 |
          +-----------------+-----------------+

                  Custom Callback Handler
                            |

              |             |             |

           Values        Duration       Event

              +-------------+-------------+
                            |
                            v
                    Structured Record
                            |
              +-------------+-------------+
              |             |             |
              v             v             v
            Logs          Metrics        Traces

Architecture Explanation

The executing LangChain component generates a lifecycle event with contextual information such as inputs, outputs, tags, metadata, run_id, and parent_run_id. The available information varies according to the component and event type.

The custom handler receives the event through the callback system and applies application-specific processing. This may include calculating elapsed time, selecting relevant fields, redacting sensitive values, counting records, or assigning an event severity.

The processed event is converted into a stable structured representation. A common record contains the event type, component name, run identifiers, duration, success status, tags, approved metadata, and sanitized error information.

The handler sends or stores the resulting record in the configured observability destination. Production applications commonly queue telemetry for background export so slow monitoring systems do not increase the latency of the user request.

d) Core Components

1. Callback Base Class

The callback base class defines the lifecycle interface that a custom handler can implement. BaseCallbackHandler supports synchronous handlers, while AsyncCallbackHandler is appropriate when the callback must perform asynchronous work such as sending telemetry through a non-blocking client.

The base handler provides no-op behavior for events that are not overridden. This allows a custom implementation to focus only on relevant model, chain, tool, retriever, agent, retry, streaming, or custom-event hooks.

2. Overridden Event Methods

Overridden methods contain the application-specific behavior performed when a matching lifecycle event occurs. A handler may store a start timestamp in on_chain_start(), calculate duration in on_chain_end(), and record a sanitized exception type in on_chain_error().

Event methods should accept **kwargs so the handler remains compatible with additional event information. Explicit keyword-only parameters such as run_id, parent_run_id, tags, and metadata can still be included when the handler uses them directly.

3. Run Correlation State

Run correlation state connects related start, completion, and failure events through a stable run identifier. A handler can store temporary information under run_id and retrieve it when the corresponding operation finishes.

Temporary run data must be cleaned up after both successful and failed executions. Failing to remove completed entries can cause memory growth in long-running services and may associate future events with stale information.

	self.start_times[run_id] = time.perf_counter()

4. Event Record

An event record is the structured representation produced by the custom callback. It should contain stable fields such as event name, run identifiers, duration, success status, component type, tags, and sanitized metadata.

The record should exclude unnecessary or sensitive data by default. Full prompts, database results, authentication headers, private documents, and raw tool outputs should be included only when permitted and required for a defined operational purpose.

5. Export Destination

The export destination receives the callback’s processed records for storage, aggregation, visualization, or alerting. Destinations may include a log collector, metric system, audit database, message queue, tracing service, or observability platform.

Production export should avoid blocking the primary request whenever possible. Queueing, asynchronous dispatch, batching, sampling, and bounded buffers help reduce callback latency and protect the application when an observability service is slow or unavailable.

e) Code Example

import time
from typing import Any
from uuid import UUID

from langchain_core.callbacks import BaseCallbackHandler
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda


SENSITIVE_KEYS = {
    "password",
    "authorization",
    "access_token",
    "api_key",
    "secret",
}


def redact_value(value: Any) -> Any:
    """
    Recursively redact sensitive dictionary fields.
    """

    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return {
            key: (
                "[REDACTED]"
                if key.lower() in SENSITIVE_KEYS
                else redact_value(item)
            )
            for key, item in value.items()
        }

    if isinstance(value, list):
        return [
            redact_value(item)
            for item in value
        ]

    if isinstance(value, tuple):
        return tuple(
            redact_value(item)
            for item in value
        )

    return value


class StructuredCallbackHandler(BaseCallbackHandler):
    """
    Capture sanitized chain lifecycle events.
    """

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()

        self.start_times: dict[UUID, float] = {}
        self.events: list[dict[str, Any]] = []

    def on_chain_start(
        self,
        serialized: dict[str, Any] | None,
        inputs: Any,
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        parent_run_id: UUID | None = None,
        tags: list[str] | None = None,
        metadata: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Record the beginning of a chain execution.
        """

        self.start_times[run_id] = time.perf_counter()

        event = {
            "event": "chain_started",
            "run_id": str(run_id),
            "parent_run_id": (
                str(parent_run_id)
                if parent_run_id is not None
                else None
            ),
            "inputs": redact_value(inputs),
            "tags": tags or [],
            "metadata": redact_value(
                metadata or {}
            ),
        }

        self.events.append(event)

    def on_chain_end(
        self,
        outputs: Any,
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        parent_run_id: UUID | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Record successful chain completion.
        """

        event = {
            "event": "chain_completed",
            "run_id": str(run_id),
            "parent_run_id": (
                str(parent_run_id)
                if parent_run_id is not None
                else None
            ),
            "success": True,
            "duration_ms": self._duration_ms(
                run_id
            ),
            "outputs": redact_value(outputs),
        }

        self.events.append(event)

    def on_chain_error(
        self,
        error: BaseException,
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        parent_run_id: UUID | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Record a failed chain execution.
        """

        event = {
            "event": "chain_failed",
            "run_id": str(run_id),
            "parent_run_id": (
                str(parent_run_id)
                if parent_run_id is not None
                else None
            ),
            "success": False,
            "duration_ms": self._duration_ms(
                run_id
            ),
            "error_type": type(error).__name__,
        }

        self.events.append(event)

    def _duration_ms(
        self,
        run_id: UUID,
    ) -> float:
        """
        Calculate duration and remove temporary data.
        """

        start_time = self.start_times.pop(
            run_id,
            time.perf_counter(),
        )

        duration_seconds = (
            time.perf_counter()
            - start_time
        )

        return round(
            duration_seconds * 1000,
            2,
        )


def process_order(
    data: dict[str, Any],
) -> dict[str, Any\]:
    """
    Calculate an order total after validating input.
    """

    quantity = int(
        data["quantity"]
    )

    unit_price = float(
        data["unit_price"]
    )

    if quantity <= 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "Quantity must be greater than zero."
        )

    if unit_price <= 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "Unit price must be greater than zero."
        )

    return {
        "order_id": data["order_id"],
        "quantity": quantity,
        "unit_price": unit_price,
        "total": round(
            quantity * unit_price,
            2,
        ),
    }


order_chain = RunnableLambda(
    process_order
).with_config(
    {
        "run_name": "process-order",
    }
)


def run_success_example(
    handler: StructuredCallbackHandler,
) -> None:
    """
    Run a successful chain invocation.
    """

    result = order_chain.invoke(
        {
            "order_id": "ORD-1001",
            "quantity": 8,
            "unit_price": 1250.0,
            "api_key": "private-api-key",
        },
        config={
            "callbacks": [
                handler,
            ],
            "tags": [
                "orders",
                "calculation",
            ],
            "metadata": {
                "request_id": "REQ-201",
                "environment": "development",
                "authorization": (
                    "Bearer private-token"
                ),
            },
        },
    )

    print(
        "Successful result:",
        result,
    )


def run_failure_example(
    handler: StructuredCallbackHandler,
) -> None:
    """
    Run a failing chain invocation.
    """

    try:
        order_chain.invoke(
            {
                "order_id": "ORD-1002",
                "quantity": 0,
                "unit_price": 1000.0,
                "password": "private-password",
            },
            config={
                "callbacks": [
                    handler,
                ],
                "tags": [
                    "orders",
                    "validation",
                ],
                "metadata": {
                    "request_id": "REQ-202",
                    "environment": "development",
                },
            },
        )

    except ValueError as error:
        print(
            "Failed execution handled:",
            str(error),
        )


def display_events(
    handler: StructuredCallbackHandler,
) -> None:
    """
    Display every captured callback event.
    """

    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("CAPTURED CALLBACK EVENTS")
    print("=" * 60)

    for position, event in enumerate(
        handler.events,
        start=1,
    ):
        print(
            f"\nEvent {position}"
        )

        print("-" * 60)

        for key, value in event.items():
            print(
                f"{key}: {value}"
            )


def main() -> None
    """
    Run the complete custom callback demonstration.
    """

    handler = StructuredCallbackHandler()

    run_success_example(
        handler
    )

    run_failure_example(
        handler
    )

    display_events(
        handler
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

redact_value() recursively examines dictionaries, lists, and tuples. When a dictionary key matches a configured sensitive name, the original value is replaced with [REDACTED].

StructuredCallbackHandler stores temporary start times and permanent event records separately. Start times are used only for duration calculation and are removed as soon as the matching end or error event arrives.

on_chain_start() records sanitized inputs, tags, metadata, and run relationships. The supplied API key and authorization value are removed before the event is stored.

on_chain_end() calculates duration and records a sanitized output. The success=True field gives monitoring logic a consistent value for aggregation.

on_chain_error() records only the exception type and duration. It avoids storing a raw error string that might contain internal data.

The callback is supplied at invocation time through config. Both the successful and failing executions use the same handler, so the final event list contains the complete observable history.


f) Interview Questions And Answers

Q1. What is a Custom Callback in LangChain?

A Custom Callback is an application-defined handler that responds to selected LangChain lifecycle events. It is created by extending BaseCallbackHandler or AsyncCallbackHandler and overriding methods for the model, chain, tool, retriever, agent, retry, token, or custom events that the application needs to observe.

Q2. Why should callback logic be separate from business logic?

Separation keeps application functions focused on their primary behavior while observability remains reusable and independently configurable. It also allows the logging, metrics, and tracing destination to change without modifying every model, tool, retriever, or chain function.

Q3. How do custom callbacks calculate execution latency?

The handler records a high-resolution timestamp during the component’s start event and stores it under the event’s run_id. When the matching end or error event arrives, the handler retrieves the timestamp, calculates the elapsed duration, and removes the temporary entry.

Q4. How should sensitive data be handled in callbacks?

Sensitive values should be removed, masked, hashed, or excluded before callback records are exported. Redaction should cover nested input fields, output fields, prompts, tool arguments, exception messages, metadata, authentication headers, personal information, and confidential documents.

Q5. What are the main production risks of Custom Callbacks?

The main risks are increased latency, excessive event volume, telemetry-export failures, concurrency problems, sensitive-data leakage, and unbounded storage growth. These should be controlled through lightweight handlers, asynchronous export, batching, sampling, thread-safe state, redaction, output limits, access control, and retention policies.

Topic 3: Logging

Logging records timestamped events generated during an LLM application’s execution. In a LangChain application, logs can capture chain starts, model calls, tool executions, retrieval activity, retries, failures, latency, and completion status, helping developers understand what happened during a particular request.

LangChain callbacks provide lifecycle hooks that can generate application logs without placing logging statements inside every chain, tool, model, and retriever function. LangSmith can complement application logging by capturing complete traces containing model interactions, tool calls, inputs, outputs, and decision points.

a) Definition

Logging is the process of recording discrete events produced while an application executes. Each log record normally contains a timestamp, severity level, event name, contextual fields, and a message describing what occurred.

In an LLM application, logging extends beyond ordinary application errors. It may record model starts and completions, selected tools, retriever activity, retries, fallback decisions, token usage, parsing failures, and final execution status.

LangChain lifecycle events can be converted into logs through callback handlers. A custom handler can observe chain, tool, model, retriever, agent, and error events and forward them to Python’s standard logging module or another logging system.

Logging is one part of observability rather than a complete observability solution. Logs provide detailed individual events, while metrics show aggregated numerical trends and traces reconstruct the complete parent-child path of one request.

b) Purpose

The primary purpose of logging is to create a searchable operational record of what an application did during execution. When a request fails or produces an unexpected result, developers can examine the relevant logs to identify which model, tool, retriever, parser, or application stage caused the problem.

Logging helps correlate events belonging to the same request across several nested operations. A shared request ID, trace ID, run ID, thread ID, or parent-run ID allows model calls, tool requests, database operations, retries, and final responses to be connected during investigation.

Logs support production monitoring and incident response by exposing failures and abnormal behavior. Operations teams can search for repeated timeout errors, unusual fallback activity, rising validation failures, unauthorized tool requests, or agents reaching their execution limits.

Logging also provides an audit trail for important system behavior when implemented with suitable security and retention controls. An application can record which operation was requested, which approved component executed it, whether it succeeded, and how long it took without logging confidential prompts, credentials, or complete private records.

c) Logging Architecture

                      LOGGING ARCHITECTURE
                      ====================

                        User Request
                             |
                             v
                     Application Runtime
                             |
             +---------------+---------------+
             |               |               |
             v               v               v
         Chain Event     Tool Event      Model Event
             |               |               |
             +---------------+---------------+
                             |
                             v
                    Callback Handler
                             |
                             v
                   Build Log Record
            Timestamp | Level | Event | Context
                             |
                             v
                      Redact Fields
                             |
                             v
                     Python Logger
                             |
                  +----------+----------+
                  |                     |
                  v                     v
          Console Handler          File Handler
                  |                     |
                  +----------+----------+
                             |
                             v
                       Log Platform
                             |
              +--------------+--------------+
              |                             |
              v                             v
          Searching                      Alerts

Architecture Explanation

LangChain components generate lifecycle events during execution. These events may include start, completion, failure, retry, token, tool, model, and retrieval information.

A callback handler receives the event and converts it into a structured log record. The handler may calculate duration, inspect tags, preserve run identifiers, and remove sensitive fields.

The record is sent to Python’s logging system using an appropriate severity level. Logging handlers then determine whether the event is written to the console, a rotating file, a remote collector, or several destinations.

A centralized log platform indexes the records for searching, dashboards, retention, and alerting. Logs should be correlated with traces and metrics using shared identifiers rather than treated as isolated text messages.

d) Logging Levels

1. DEBUG:- Detailed diagnostic information used during development.

Suitable examples: Sanitized tool arguments, Routing decisions, Retrieved document count, Parsed output type, Intermediate state changes
DEBUG logs can be highly detailed and should usually be disabled or sampled in production.

2. INFO:- Normal execution events confirming system progress.

Normal execution events confirming system progress.
Suitable examples: Request started, Chain completed, Tool executed successfully, Fallback selected, Human approval received.

3. WARNING:- An unusual condition occurred, but execution can continue.

Suitable examples: Primary service failed and fallback was used, Retry was scheduled, Retrieval returned no documents, Context usage approached a configured threshold, Deprecated functionality was invoked.

4. ERROR:- An operation failed and the current task could not continue normally.

Suitable examples: Tool execution failed, Model provider returned an error, Output parsing failed, Database lookup could not complete, Retry limit was exhausted.

5. CRITICAL:- A severe failure threatens the availability, security, or integrity of the application.

Suitable examples: Persistent checkpoint corruption, Widespread provider failure, Potential credential exposure, Production database unavailable, Essential dependency cannot start.

e) Core Components

1. Logger

A logger receives application log records and assigns them to a named logging category. Using a module or application-specific logger is preferable to relying directly on the root logger because levels and handlers can be configured independently. 

The logger evaluates the configured severity threshold before forwarding a record to its handlers. For example, an INFO configuration records informational, warning, error, and critical events while ignoring debug records.\

	import logging

	logger = logging.getLogger("order_agent")
	logger.setLevel( logging.INFO)

2. Log Handler

A log handler determines where accepted records are sent. Common destinations include the console, files, rotating files, system log services, message queues, and centralized observability platforms.

Several handlers can be attached to one logger with different levels and formats. Development diagnostics may go to the console, while production errors are simultaneously sent to a persistent log destination.

console_handler = logging.StreamHandler()
logger.addHandler( console_handler )

3. Formatter

A formatter determines how each record is represented at the selected destination. It may produce readable text for local development or JSON-like structured output for centralized production logging.

The format should include enough correlation context to support investigation. Useful fields include timestamp, severity, logger name, event type, request ID, run ID, component name, and execution duration.

formatter = logging.Formatter(
    "%(asctime)s | %(levelname)s | "
    "%(name)s | %(message)s"
)


4. Callback Logging Handler

A callback logging handler converts LangChain lifecycle events into ordinary application log records. It can observe chain, tool, model, retriever, retry, and error hooks without adding logging statements inside the components themselves.

The callback should record sanitized operational context rather than unrestricted inputs and outputs. Raw prompts, private database records, authorization headers, and complete documents should normally be excluded, summarized, or redacted.

5. Correlation Context

Correlation context connects log records generated by the same application request. Values such as request_id, run_id, parent_run_id, trace_id, and thread_id make it possible to reconstruct activity across nested components.

Correlation identifiers should be generated or validated by trusted application code. They should not contain confidential data, and user-supplied values should not be accepted blindly as authoritative identifiers.

f) Code Example

import json
import logging
import time
from logging.handlers import RotatingFileHandler
from typing import Any
from uuid import UUID
from langchain_core.callbacks import BaseCallbackHandler
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda


LOG_FILE = "application.log"

SENSITIVE_KEYS = {
    "password",
    "authorization",
    "access_token",
    "api_key",
    "secret",
}


def redact_value(value: Any) -> Any:
    """
    Recursively redact configured sensitive fields.
    """

    if isinstance(value, dict):
        sanitized = {}

        for key, item in value.items():
            if key.lower() in SENSITIVE_KEYS:
                sanitized[key] = "[REDACTED]"
            else:
                sanitized[key] = redact_value(
                    item
                )

        return sanitized

    if isinstance(value, list):
        return [
            redact_value(item)
            for item in value
        ]

    if isinstance(value, tuple):
        return tuple(
            redact_value(item)
            for item in value
        )

    return value


def configure_logger() -> logging.Logger:
    """
    Configure console and rotating file logging.
    """

    logger = logging.getLogger(
        "order_application"
    )

    logger.setLevel(
        logging.INFO
    )

    logger.propagate = False

    if logger.handlers:
        return logger

    formatter = logging.Formatter(
        "%(asctime)s | %(levelname)s | "
        "%(name)s | %(message)s"
    )

    console_handler = logging.StreamHandler()

    console_handler.setLevel(
        logging.INFO
    )

    console_handler.setFormatter(
        formatter
    )

    file_handler = RotatingFileHandler(
        LOG_FILE,
        maxBytes=1_000_000,
        backupCount=3,
        encoding="utf-8",
    )

    file_handler.setLevel(
        logging.INFO
    )

    file_handler.setFormatter(
        formatter
    )

    logger.addHandler(
        console_handler
    )

    logger.addHandler(
        file_handler
    )

    return logger


class LoggingCallbackHandler(
    BaseCallbackHandler
):
    """
    Convert chain lifecycle events into structured logs.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        logger: logging.Logger,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__()

        self.logger = logger

        self.start_times: dict[
            UUID,
            float,
        ] = {}

        self.run_context: dict[
            UUID,
            dict[str, Any],
        ] = {}

    def on_chain_start(
        self,
        serialized: dict[str, Any] | None,
        inputs: Any,
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        parent_run_id: UUID | None = None,
        tags: list[str] | None = None,
        metadata: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        self.start_times[run_id] = (
            time.perf_counter()
        )

        safe_metadata = redact_value(
            metadata or {}
        )

        self.run_context[run_id] = {
            "request_id": safe_metadata.get(
                "request_id"
            )
        }

        self._log(
            logging.INFO,
            {
                "event": "chain_started",
                "run_id": str(run_id),
                "parent_run_id": self._uuid_text(
                    parent_run_id
                ),
                "request_id": safe_metadata.get(
                    "request_id"
                ),
                "tags": tags or [],
                "inputs": redact_value(inputs),
            },
        )

    def on_chain_end(
        self,
        outputs: Any,
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        parent_run_id: UUID | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        context = self.run_context.pop(
            run_id,
            {},
        )

        self._log(
            logging.INFO,
            {
                "event": "chain_completed",
                "run_id": str(run_id),
                "parent_run_id": self._uuid_text(
                    parent_run_id
                ),
                "request_id": context.get(
                    "request_id"
                ),
                "success": True,
                "duration_ms": self._duration_ms(
                    run_id
                ),
                "outputs": redact_value(outputs),
            },
        )

    def on_chain_error(
        self,
        error: BaseException,
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        parent_run_id: UUID | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        context = self.run_context.pop(
            run_id,
            {},
        )

        self._log(
            logging.ERROR,
            {
                "event": "chain_failed",
                "run_id": str(run_id),
                "parent_run_id": self._uuid_text(
                    parent_run_id
                ),
                "request_id": context.get(
                    "request_id"
                ),
                "success": False,
                "duration_ms": self._duration_ms(
                    run_id
                ),
                "error_type": type(error).__name__,
            },
        )

    def _duration_ms(
        self,
        run_id: UUID,
    ) -> float:
        start_time = self.start_times.pop(
            run_id,
            time.perf_counter(),
        )

        duration = (
            time.perf_counter()
            - start_time
        ) * 1000

        return round(
            duration,
            2,
        )

    def _log(
        self,
        level: int,
        event: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> None:
        self.logger.log(
            level,
            json.dumps(
                event,
                ensure_ascii=False,
                default=str,
            ),
        )

    @staticmethod
    def _uuid_text(
        value: UUID | None,
    ) -> str | None:
        if value is None:
            return None

        return str(value)


def process_order(
    data: dict[str, Any],
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Validate and calculate an order total.
    """

    quantity = int(
        data["quantity"]
    )

    unit_price = float(
        data["unit_price"]
    )

    if quantity <= 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "Quantity must be greater than zero."
        )

    if unit_price <= 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "Unit price must be greater than zero."
        )

    return {
        "order_id": data["order_id"],
        "quantity": quantity,
        "unit_price": unit_price,
        "total": round(
            quantity * unit_price,
            2,
        ),
    }


order_chain = RunnableLambda(
    process_order
).with_config(
    {
        "run_name": "process-order",
    }
)


def run_successful_request(
    callback: LoggingCallbackHandler,
) -> None:
    """
    Execute one successful request.
    """

    result = order_chain.invoke(
        {
            "order_id": "ORD-1001",
            "quantity": 8,
            "unit_price": 1250.0,
            "api_key": "private-api-key",
        },
        config={
            "callbacks": [
                callback,
            ],
            "tags": [
                "orders",
                "calculation",
            ],
            "metadata": {
                "request_id": "REQ-301",
                "environment": "development",
                "authorization": (
                    "Bearer private-token"
                ),
            },
        },
    )

    print(
        "Successful result:",
        result,
    )


def run_failed_request(
    callback: LoggingCallbackHandler,
) -> None:
    """
    Execute one request that fails validation.
    """

    try:
        order_chain.invoke(
            {
                "order_id": "ORD-1002",
                "quantity": 0,
                "unit_price": 1000.0,
                "password": "private-password",
            },
            config={
                "callbacks": [
                    callback,
                ],
                "tags": [
                    "orders",
                    "validation",
                ],
                "metadata": {
                    "request_id": "REQ-302",
                    "environment": "development",
                },
            },
        )

    except ValueError:
        print(
            "Failed request was safely handled."
        )


def main() -> None:
    """
    Run the complete logging demonstration.
    """

    logger = configure_logger()

    callback = LoggingCallbackHandler(
        logger
    )

    run_successful_request(
        callback
    )

    run_failed_request(
        callback
    )

    print(
        f"Logs were also written to {LOG_FILE}."
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Code Explanation

configure_logger() creates one application logger with console and rotating-file handlers. The handler guard prevents repeated calls from adding duplicate output handlers.

LoggingCallbackHandler converts LangChain chain events into structured dictionaries. Each dictionary is serialized using json.dumps() before being sent to Python’s logging system.

on_chain_start() records the request ID, run identifiers, tags, and sanitized inputs. The API key and authorization value are replaced before they are exported.

on_chain_end() records successful completion, elapsed time, and the sanitized result. Temporary timing and contextual state are removed after the event is created.

on_chain_error() records the exception type without exporting the raw exception text. The application catches the original exception separately and controls the user-facing behavior.

The rotating file handler controls local file growth. When the configured size is reached, older files are retained only up to backupCount.

g) Interview Questions and Answers

Q1. What is logging in an LLM application?

Logging is the process of recording timestamped events generated while models, tools, retrievers, chains, and agents execute. The records help developers debug failures, track performance, investigate abnormal behavior, and maintain an operational history.

Q2. What is structured logging?

Structured logging represents each event through stable named fields instead of one unstructured text sentence. Typical fields include the event name, request ID, run ID, component, duration, success status, error type, model, tool, tags, and approved metadata.

Q3. How can LangChain callbacks be used for logging?

A developer can extend BaseCallbackHandler and override lifecycle methods such as on_chain_start(), on_chain_end(), on_tool_start(), or on_tool_error(). The handler converts callback data into log records and forwards those records to Python logging or another system.

Q4. What information should not be logged?

Logs should not contain passwords, API keys, access tokens, authorization headers, database credentials, private customer records, confidential documents, or unrestricted prompt content. Sensitive values should be redacted or omitted before records are sent to any logging destination.

Q5. What is the difference between logs and traces?

Logs record individual events, such as a tool failure or model completion. Traces reconstruct the full hierarchical path of one request, showing how the parent agent run includes child model calls, tool operations, retrieval calls, and other steps. LangSmith can capture this full execution structure for LangChain agents.

Topic 4: Monitoring

Monitoring continuously measures the operational health, performance, usage, reliability, and quality of an LLM application. It converts callback events, logs, traces, model responses, token metadata, tool outcomes, and user feedback into metrics that can be visualized through dashboards and evaluated through alerts.

Unlike ordinary service monitoring, agent monitoring must also track multi-step behavior such as tool selection, retrieval quality, repeated actions, agent iterations, fallbacks, human interventions, token usage, and response quality. A request may complete without raising an exception while still returning irrelevant documents, selecting the wrong tool, or producing an unsupported answer.

a) Definition

Monitoring is the continuous collection and evaluation of known operational signals that describe whether an LLM application is functioning within expected limits. These signals commonly include request volume, success rate, failure rate, latency, model calls, tool calls, retries, token usage, estimated cost, fallback activity, and human escalations.

Monitoring differs from one-time debugging because it operates continuously across many application executions. Instead of examining only one failed request, monitoring aggregates measurements over time to reveal patterns such as increasing model latency, declining tool reliability, rising token consumption, or repeated agent loops.

LLM and agent monitoring must measure both traditional infrastructure health and AI-specific behavior. A service may return HTTP success responses while its retriever returns irrelevant documents, its model selects incorrect tools, or its answers gradually lose quality, so ordinary uptime and CPU metrics are not sufficient.

Monitoring is usually implemented by converting application events into counters, gauges, histograms, and evaluation scores. These measurements are aggregated into dashboards, compared with thresholds or service objectives, and used to generate alerts when behavior becomes abnormal.

b) Purpose

The primary purpose of monitoring is to detect operational and quality problems before they affect a large number of users. A dashboard or alert can reveal that model latency has increased, a database tool has started timing out, retrieval is returning empty results, or an agent is repeatedly using fallback services even when the application still appears available.

Monitoring allows teams to understand long-term trends rather than investigating each request independently. By aggregating measurements by application, model, tool, tenant, environment, and time period, teams can identify whether performance, reliability, quality, token usage, or cost is improving or deteriorating.

It helps control unpredictable resource consumption in agentic applications. Multi-step agents may call models and tools repeatedly, so monitoring model-call counts, tool-call counts, iterations, tokens, cost, retries, and execution duration helps teams detect runaway loops and inefficient workflows.

Monitoring also supports measurable service objectives and automated operational response. Teams can define acceptable targets for availability, latency, tool success rate, answer quality, human-escalation rate, or cost per request, then notify operators when those indicators cross warning or critical thresholds. LangSmith supports monitoring costs, latency, response quality, production traces, and alerting for agent behavior.

c) Monitoring Architecture

               |                             |

        Trend Analysis              Operator Notification
